object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A tracked event representing something that broke, from declaration through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal, automated or manually raised, indicating something may be wrong; comes from the monitoring platform (or a manual raise).

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, potentially linked to an incident as its origin.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A classification of blast radius and technical impact, from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, one region).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A classification of customer urgency -- who's affected, SLA breach risk -- from P1 to P4.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Commander
object_types.definition: The named person acting as incident commander for the duration of a declared incident; a role, not a job title.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: CommanderName
object_types.definition: The name identifying the person acting as incident commander.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A service in the catalogue that can be affected by incidents and is owned by a team.

ambiguities.description: The 'duplicate of' rule is described as intended but explicitly stated as not enforced by the system today (no chain prevention, primaries can still have a duplicate-of link). Should the acyclic/no-chain constraint be modeled as a hard rule or only as a documented intent, given it is violated in practice?

source_references.excerpt: But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Whether a customer-caused incident (later found to be user error/misconfiguration) should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and parked for a separate stakeholder (Ravi). No 'cause classification' concept currently exists in the system, so none was modeled -- but this is a known gap that may require a future object type/fact type.

source_references.excerpt: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' term mentioned by Owen as sitting between mitigated and resolved was explicitly rejected as a formal state ('not in the dropdown'). Confirm this is purely informal chatter and never needs modeling, versus being an emerging state that should eventually be added.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius'), with history captured only informally 'in the timeline, as events,' not as a structured fact type. The model captures only the current value. Should a formal history/timeline entity be modeled to track severity/priority changes over time?

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged by both Nadia and Owen as ambiguous/overloaded in everyday usage -- it can mean either the Incident Commander (temporary role) or the Service Owner (standing team assignment). The model distinguishes these as separate fact types (Commander runs Incident vs Team owns Service), but stakeholders confirm the term itself causes real confusion in practice; ensure downstream consumers of the model do not conflate the two.

source_references.excerpt: The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing. That's a standing assignment, nothing to do with the incident. ... And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are also referred to colloquially as 'sev' for both terms interchangeably, causing miscommunication ('Somebody says we've got a sev one... and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager'). This is a terminology/communication issue rather than a modeling gap, but worth flagging since it could indicate inconsistent data entry or reporting if the same colloquial term is used to populate either field.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.

ambiguities.description: Commander is identified only by a name ('CommanderName'), which may not be a reliable unique identifier for a person across the organization (e.g., two commanders could share a name). No formal employee ID or similar was discussed; confirm whether a more robust identifier exists for commanders/engineers.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.
